One blockchain. Two assets. Why?

At first glance, using two assets on one blockchain might seem unnecessarily complicated.

Why not use one asset for everything?

To understand DAC’s approach, we need to look at the different roles its two assets perform.

<> DACT: Network participation

DACT is the @dac_chain token associated with staking and activating Validator and Supervisor Nodes. These nodes participate in the network’s operations and consensus process.

DACT is also associated with access to certain DAC services.

<> DACC: Network transactions

DACC is the native currency of the DAC blockchain. It is used to pay transaction fees and execute smart contracts. The published architecture also identifies it as a reward for network nodes.

The distinction is about function.

DACT is connected to participation in the network, while DACC is used to pay for activity carried out on the blockchain.

<> Why separate the two?

A blockchain has different economic requirements.

It needs participants to operate and support the network. It also needs a currency for processing transactions and executing applications.

DAC’s dual-asset model assigns these functions to different assets rather than combining them into one.

The architecture also describes conversion between DACT and DACC, linking the two parts of the system.

But separating the assets does not, by itself, prove that transaction fees will remain predictable or that the network will be more efficient. Those outcomes depend on the actual design and operation of the system.

The useful question is not simply why DAC has two assets.

It is how the relationship between them works: how network participation is supported, how transaction costs are determined, and how DACT and DACC interact.

That is where the details of a dual-asset model matter.

Two assets, distinct roles, one network.

Netanyahu supporters seem to be taking advantage of @Brett_McGurk’s book and interviews to claim vindication for Netanyahu’s conduct of the war in Gaza. But while Brett’s front-row account is valuable, that doesn’t mean it is definitive or its perspectives widely shared—including among former members of the Biden administration.

I would say most of my former colleagues think that President Biden should have put more pressure on Israel to conduct the war differently and end it sooner, and few think that the biggest mistake Biden made was to show daylight with Israel. And even Brett’s account makes clear that hostages were not the top priority for Netanyahu and that when U.S. pressure actually was applied—as after the World Central Kitchen strike—it worked.

Brett tells the story of the Biden phone call after that tragedy, but not the story of how Biden called Netanyahu on July 4, 2024 to press him to conclude the hostage deal after Hamas had finally accepted the basic framework, dropping its demand that Israel commit to a permanent ceasefire before any hostages were released. Netanyahu instead added so many of his own conditions—against the advice of his own security chiefs—that the deal became impossible for another six months, during which nearly 9,000 more Palestinians were killed and more Israeli hostages died, including the six that Hamas executed in August. The Israeli changes included a demand that Israel retain forces along Gaza’s entire border with Egypt, which the IDF had seized only after the original proposal, and a new enforcement mechanism to screen Gazans who were returning home to the north which would have required Israeli troops to remain in central Gaza. Both of those new conditions were dropped in the deal ultimately concluded in January 2025.

Nothing in the book or elsewhere changes the reality that October 7 happened on Netanyahu’s watch; that he prioritized “total victory” and the maintenance of his coalition over a hostage deal or an end of the war; that his conduct of the war and management of its humanitarian consequences catastrophic; that it has left Israel more isolated and insecure; and that it has deeply damaged, perhaps irreparably, Israel’s relationship with the United States—which should have done more to change Israel’s conduct rather than enable it. There was never an easy way forward in Gaza, but no version of the story vindicates Netanyahu.

Something feels off with this chorus of “India’s internet is great and super cheap” … the data shows that Indian market is absolutely dominated by mobile. When they say it’s cheap and well connected factually this only applies to mobile usage. 

This makes sense because a tower connects thousands of subs instantly after construction and running fiber is a building by building or resident by resident job. This is also why “fixed wireless” has started growing fast. Follow the incentives. It’s the cheapest and shortest route to revenue. 

Due to this, India is amongst the highest mobile bandwidth usage populations on the planet. 30-40GB/month. (20-50% above US/UK usage) However, home Fiber lines in India pull closer to 300GB/month. 10x gap

For context, that gap in the US and UK is 20-30x. It’s pretty ubiquitous that if you have access to a lot of more bandwidth you will use it. 

Bandwidth abundance does not favor mobile devices. 

I’d argue that it’s not very hard to believe that these paltry sub 5% fixed customer penetration numbers would be much higher if a cost effective alternative existed.

Is that alternative existed it wouldn’t be crazy to expect to see the fixed customer numbers jump from 6% to maybe 10%, 15% or 20%. 100M-200M customers. 

And if the rest of the world is any precedent that would lead to a dramatic increase in overall bandwidth used. 

However, that would mean that mobile bandwidth usage would likely drop or stagnate with in home mobile usage.

What actually changes when a blockchain prepares for quantum computing?

Quantum readiness is more than replacing one cryptographic algorithm with another. To understand why, we need to look at how blockchain security works and where quantum computing could affect it.

1. Start with cryptographic assumptions

Blockchains rely on mathematical problems that are difficult for conventional computers to solve. Some cryptographic systems use these problems to protect keys and verify digital signatures.

A sufficiently powerful quantum computer could break certain assumptions behind existing public-key cryptography. This does not mean every part of a blockchain would automatically become vulnerable.

2. What happens to wallet security?

A wallet uses cryptographic keys to authorise transactions. Digital signatures allow the network to check that a transaction was approved by someone with the required private key.

If the signature scheme becomes vulnerable to quantum attacks, an attacker could potentially forge signatures and spend assets without the owner's permission.

This is why protecting the relationship between private keys, public keys and digital signatures matters.

3. How does this affect transactions?

Every transaction must pass the network's authorisation checks.

If the cryptographic method used to verify a signature is no longer secure, the network may struggle to distinguish a legitimate transaction from a forged one.

Preparing for quantum computing therefore involves more than protecting wallets. It also means considering how transactions will be authenticated under new cryptographic standards.

4. Why do long-term records matter?

Blockchains are designed to preserve transaction histories and ownership records over time.

Even if an asset is secure today, its security requirements may change during its lifetime. Migration procedures, old signatures and previously exposed public keys may all need consideration when upgrading cryptography.

A blockchain must think about how to maintain security across these transitions, not just how to protect new transactions.

5. Where does DAC fit into this?

@dac_chain  Chain's approach centres on treating quantum resistance as an infrastructure-level design consideration rather than simply a feature to add when the threat becomes immediate.

The broader engineering question is how cryptographic protection fits into the blockchain's architecture and how that protection can be maintained as security requirements evolve.

Quantum-resistant cryptography is not a guarantee against every possible attack. It is a way to address specific future risks by using cryptographic methods designed to withstand known quantum computing attacks.

The lesson is simple: preparing a blockchain for quantum computing means examining the assumptions behind its security today and planning how those protections can remain reliable in the future.
